newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Bank staff down tools over South African crime.
newsitem.headline: Bank staff down tools over South African crime.

text.p: South Africa's leading banks shut for two hours in major centres on Thursday to allow an estimated 50,000 staff around the country to protest against the spiralling crime rate.

Bank tellers and other employees held peaceful marches in at least nine centres calling on the government to introduce more effective measures to protect them at work and counter a rash of armed robberies in the past year.

The Council of South African Banks (Cosab), representing all large banks in the country, backed the protests with full-page newspaper advertisements depicting video-camera footage of a robbery in progress, stating:
"After all our staff have been through in the last few months, we're sure you wouldn't begrudge them two hours of protest."
Police figures show 1.8 million crimes were reported in South Africa during 1996, and banks say robberies cost the industry some $25 million a year.

Ben Venter, a spokesman for Sasbo -- the Finance Union which organised the day of protest -- told Reuters that 164 armed bank robberies had taken place so far this year in which many of its members had been hurt or killed.
"Something must be done against organised crime. Gangsters must be removed from society," Venter said.
The former ruling National Party, reacting to the protests, accused the government of doing too little to combat crime.

"The fact that the banking fraternity decided to close their doors today during the lunch hour must be seen as a desperate effort to bring to the attention of the authorities that crime is getting out of hand," the party said in a statement.
Violent crime has soared since President Nelson Mandela's African Nationl Congress (ANC) won the country's first all-race elections in 1994.
The marches coincided with an announcement by Policing Minister Sydney Mufamadi that the government would with immediate effect lift a 1994 moratorium on new police recruits.

Mufamadi said almost 150 million rand ($33 million) would be spent on hiring 5,250 civilian and uniformed officers to beef up crime prevention along the country's borders, forensics skills, child abuse unit and other priority areas.
